query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin silicide-based coating (e.g., a Si-20Cr-20Fe layer) onto a refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) will improve its high-temperature oxygen resistance by promoting the formation of a dense, adherent protective oxide scale that inhibits further oxygen ingress.
generation.material_initial_state: A bulk refractory high-entropy alloy such as MoNbTaTiW produced by conventional processing methods, which in its untreated state exhibits significant oxidation (e.g., high oxide weight gain and spallation) when exposed to extreme high-temperature air.
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin, uniform silicide coating (for example, a Si-20Cr-20Fe coating applied via a fused slurry or similar method) on the RHEA surface.
generation.conditions: Exposure at high temperature (around 1200 °C) in an oxygen-containing atmosphere (ambient air) for an extended period (e.g., 10 hours) under static or controlled flow conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The silicide coating reacts during high-temperature exposure to form a continuous and dense protective oxide layer (likely rich in silica and related compounds) that adheres to the substrate.
generation.mechanism: By forming a silicide-derived oxide scale, the coating acts as a diffusion barrier, slowing down the penetration of oxygen into the alloy and thereby reducing oxidation-induced degradation without affecting the bulk mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to an untreated RHEA, the coated alloy is predicted to show a significantly lower oxide weight gain and no catastrophic scale spallation after exposure, thus preserving its surface integrity and contributing to improved high-temperature performance.
generation.baseline: Untreated refractory HEAs typically develop thick, non-adherent oxide layers with significant material loss and spallation when exposed to 1200 °C in air for extended periods.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective under static high-temperature oxidation conditions (around 1200 °C in ambient air), but its performance under extreme thermal cycling or in highly oxidizing environments (e.g., very high oxygen pressures) requires further investigation.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of the improvement in oxidation resistance and the long-term adhesion/stability of the silicide-derived oxide scale under cyclic thermal stresses remain uncertain and need to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same refractory HEA (e.g., MoNbTaTiW). One set receives the silicide coating (Si-20Cr-20Fe) while the other set remains uncoated (control). Subject both sets to a 10-hour oxidation test at 1200 °C in ambient air. Post-treatment, assess the samples by measuring oxide weight gain, evaluating scale adhesion, and performing microstructural analyses.
measurements: Mass change (oxide weight gain) via thermogravimetric analysis
Surface and cross-sectional microscopy (SEM) to observe scale morphology and spallation
X-ray diffraction (XRD) to characterize the oxide phases formed
Adhesion tests (e.g., scratch or pull-off tests) to assess coating integrity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the silicide-coated RHEA does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxide weight gain, or if the protective scale shows extensive spallation or degradation comparable to or worse than the uncoated counterpart after 10 hours at 1200 °C in air, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) represent a new class of alloys that consist of more than four alloying elements in close to equiatomic concentrations (). The diverse compositional possibilities of HEAs, combined with appropriate heat treatment conditions, offer the potential to develop new alloys with a combination of remarkable properties such as outstanding mechanical properties, high-hydrogen absorption capacity, and robust resistance to corrosion and radiation (). The refractory HEAs (RHEAs) based on refractory elements were proposed by Senkov et al. () as a new class of high-temperature structural alloys that might surpass the capabilities of nickel-based superalloys. RHEAs are emerging as prominent contenders in diverse industries, notably in the nuclear and aerospace sectors (, ).

AbstractIn this paper, the Si-20Cr-20Fe coating was prepared on MoNbTaTiW RHEA by a fused slurry method. The microstructural evolution and compositions of the silicide coating under high-temperature oxidation environment were studied. The results show that the silicide coating could effectively prevent the oxidation of the MoNbTaTiW RHEA. The initial silicide coating had a double-layer structure: a high silicon content layer mainly composed of MSi2 as the outer layer and a low silicon content layer mainly contained M5Si3 as the inner layer. Under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the silicon element diffused from the silicide coating to the RHEA substrate while the oxidation of the coating occurred. After oxidation, the coating was composed of an outer oxide layer and an inner silicide layer. The silicide layer moved toward the inside of the substrate, led to the increase of its thickness. Compared with the initial silicified layer, its structure did not change significantly. The structure and compositions of the oxide layer on the outer surface strongly depended on the oxidation temperature. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are considered to be a new generation of high-temperature materials, because they have the advantages of both high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and refractory metals (RMs), such as high-temperature strength, high hardness, and good phase stability at high temperatures [,,,,,,]. They are mainly composed of Mo, Nb, Ta, and W, while Ti, Cr, V, Si, and Al are usually used as strengthening alloy elements [,,,,,,]. For example, Mo25Nb25Ta25W25 and Mo20Nb20Ta20W20V20 are two of the types of most extensively studied RHEAs []. The neutron diffraction analysis of those alloys after annealing at 1400 °C for 19 h shows that no changes have occurred to their phase structures. Their compression yield strengths are much higher than that of Inconel 718 alloy at temperatures above 800 °C. Furthermore, their yield strengths are still higher than 500 MPa at 1200 °C [,].
